Autoresearch

Point Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse at a problem and let it grind while you sleep.

The idea comes from Karpathy's autoresearch: one constraint, one mechanical metric, iteration that never stops. The gains stack.

Set the GOAL. The agent runs the LOOP. You wake up to results.

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that won't quit.

All five agents (Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, Muse) work for the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush: metric loops escape plateaus the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness); the other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it answers with FORK before giving up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee

Bumblebee collects package, extension, and developer-tool metadata from macOS and Linux developer endpoints. It reads. It never writes.

Here's the question it answers: an advisory just dropped and names a package, extension, or version. Which of your developer machines have a match sitting in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Neither helps when you need to see the messy local state on a developer machine: lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee reads that scattered state and turns it into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches. If you already know what you're hunting, you get a fast, read-only exposure check. Nothing on disk changes.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across different domains. It measures how much a model improves at solving complex real-world tasks when given specialized Skills.

We adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting to test performance in production-like environments where many Skills are installed at once. In the original setup, each task comes with only the specialized Skill tied to that task. In our modified version, every task is evaluated in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, with all other experimental conditions unchanged. The point is to see whether an agent can find, select, and orchestrate the right Skills from a large installed pool and organize them into a workflow that completes complex tasks.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, cut token consumption by 29.6%, and reduced tool calls by 33.1%.
